steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Tectonic: plate boundaries; Climatic: atmospheric; Geomorphological: slope failure

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Risk = Hazard x Vulnerability / Capacity to cope; PAR model (Pressure And Release)

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Evidence: Keeling curve, IPCC reports, proxy data (ice cores, tree rings); GHG: CO₂, CH₄, N₂O

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Impacts: sea level rise (thermal expansion, ice melt), extreme weather, biome shifts, ocean acidification

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Q: Explain why vulnerability is a key component of hazard risk --- Solution: Same magnitude earthquake: Haiti 2010 (M7.0, 230k deaths) vs Chile 2010 (M8.8, 500 deaths). Haiti: poor building codes, dense informal housing, weak governance -> high vulnerability. Chile: strict codes, preparedness, wealth -> low vulnerability. Risk depends on vulnerability not just hazard

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Classify 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami | Explain greenhouse effect mechanism | Compare adaptation vs mitigation examples

steps.title: Lesson plan
steps.body: Starter (5 min): Recall prior knowledge of hazards and global issues with quick questions. Teaching (15 min): Work through each of the learning objectives, explaining principles step by step. Key points review (5 min): Revisit the key points together, confirming understanding. Worked example (10 min): Model the example question: Explain why vulnerability is a key component of hazard risk. Solution: Same magnitude earthquake: Haiti 2010 (M7.0, 230k deaths) vs Chile 2010 (M8.8, 500 deaths). Haiti: poor building codes, dense informal housing, weak governance -> high vulnerability. Chile: strict codes, preparedness, wealth -> low vulnerability. Risk depends on vulnerability not just hazard Practice (10 min): Students attempt the practice questions independently; circulate and support. Plenary
